records.sourceFile: Running speed increases plantar load more than per cent body weight on an AlterG® treadmill.pdf

paper.citation: Thomson A, Einarsson E, Witvrouw E, Whiteley R. Running speed increases plantar load more than per cent body weight on an AlterG® treadmill. J Sports Sci. 2017;35(3):277-282.
paper.abstract: Twenty male runners ran on an AlterG treadmill across 36 combinations of speed (6 to 16 km/h) and indicated bodyweight (50 to 100%), while in-shoe peak plantar force was recorded.
paper.tldr: On an anti-gravity treadmill, raising running speed loads the foot far more than raising the bodyweight setting. Treat speed changes as the big load step and bodyweight changes as the small one, and check the table before stepping up.
paper.methods: Twenty injury-free male runners completed all 36 speed and bodyweight conditions in random order on an AlterG treadmill. Peak plantar force was recorded with Pedar-X in-shoe insoles and normalised to bodyweight.
paper.findings: Peak force rose from 1.02 BW at 6 km/h and 50% indicated BW to 2.31 BW at 16 km/h and 100%. In Table 1, the speed effect at fixed bodyweight (about 0.75 to 1.10 BW) was larger than the bodyweight effect at fixed speed (about 0.19 to 0.56 BW). Speed related to peak force on a logarithmic curve and bodyweight on a linear one.
paper.limitations: Healthy male participants wearing their own shoes only. Sampling at 100 Hz may miss true peaks, and only the vertical force component was measured. The abstract and Table 2 give smaller ranges (0.74 to 0.91 BW for speed, 0.19 to 0.31 BW for bodyweight) than the absolute differences in Table 1 and the discussion. The authors caution that over-ground running loads are higher than treadmill values.
paper.practicalImplications: Table 1 can guide stepwise progression of plantar loading across speed and bodyweight combinations on an AlterG treadmill. The authors suggest walking below 6 km/h at 50% indicated BW if plantar load must stay under 1 BW early in rehabilitation.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Speed steps on an anti-gravity treadmill change plantar load far more than bodyweight steps, so speed is the main lever for graded running load. The paper measured no performance outcome.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The table can help grade plantar loading during rehabilitation before running, but the paper does not show that these loads predict readiness or re-injury. It cannot be used alone to clear an athlete for sport.

paper.citation: Johnson AK, Recchia R, Tayfur A, Krishnan C, Palmieri-Smith RM. Speeding Up or Slowing Down: The Effect of Decoupling Speed on Knee Biomechanics and Limb Loading During Split-Belt Treadmill Training in Persons With ACL Reconstruction. Am J Sports Med. 2025.
paper.abstract: Controlled laboratory study of 24 people after ACL reconstruction walking on a split-belt treadmill, with the operated-leg belt set at eight speeds from 30% to 170% of 1.1 m/s.
paper.tldr: Changing the speed of the operated-leg belt changes knee and limb loading in a graded way. Faster speeds raised early-stance loading and slower speeds raised midstance loading, so the speed chosen matters.
paper.methods: Participants walked on an instrumented split-belt treadmill with 3D motion capture. After a tied-belt baseline at 1.1 m/s, eight 5-minute decoupled-speed conditions were run in random order, with 2 minutes of tied-belt walking between them. Knee moments, angles and vertical ground-reaction forces were compared with baseline using statistical parametric mapping.
paper.findings: Operated-leg speeds of 130% to 170% increased early-stance peak knee moment and peak vertical force in both limbs, while 30% and 50% decreased them. Slower speeds (30% to 90%) raised midstance knee moment and vertical load, and faster speeds lowered them. Simple linear models fitted the peak and midstance relationships, which the authors describe as dose-response, while second peak vertical force fitted a fourth-order polynomial.
paper.limitations: Participants did not show the expected baseline loading asymmetry. The 2-minute washout may not have cleared prior effects, although speeds were randomised. Most participants had patellar tendon grafts, and the design cannot show aftereffects or transfer to overground walking.
paper.practicalImplications: Split-belt speed is a dose that can be set to raise or lower knee and limb loading during treadmill walking. The authors suggest slower (30% to 50%) or faster (150% to 170%) operated-leg speeds as options to explore, not as proven protocols.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: No performance outcome was measured. The findings concern loading during rehabilitation walking only.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study suggests split-belt speed can change knee loading during rehabilitation, but it cannot show that the effect lasts after training or transfers to overground walking or return to sport. The acute loading changes should not be used as a return-to-sport criterion.

records.sourceFile: Self-Reported Fear Predicts              Functional Performance and Second ACL Injury After ACL       Reconstruction     and    Return to Sport- A Pilot Study.pdf

paper.citation: Paterno MV, Flynn K, Thomas S, Schmitt LC. Self-Reported Fear Predicts Functional Performance and Second ACL Injury After ACL Reconstruction and Return to Sport: A Pilot Study. Sports Health. 2017.
paper.abstract: Prospective cohort pilot of 40 patients cleared to return to sport after ACL reconstruction. Fear was measured with the TSK-11 at return to sport and compared with activity level, single-leg hop and quadriceps limb symmetry, and second ACL injury over 24 months. High-fear patients (TSK-11 of 17 or more) were more likely to have lower activity and hop and quadriceps asymmetry. A TSK-11 score of 19 or more was associated with a higher risk of ipsilateral second ACL tear within 24 months.
paper.tldr: Athletes returning from ACL reconstruction who reported high fear at clearance were less active, had more hop and quadriceps asymmetry, and had more same-side second ACL injuries. The paper suggests fear may belong in discharge criteria, but this 40-patient pilot cannot set a release threshold.
paper.methods: Forty patients aged 10 to 25 who had been cleared to return to pivoting and cutting sports after primary ACL reconstruction were tested within four weeks of clearance. Testing included the TSK-11, the Marx Activity Rating Scale, four single-leg hop tests and isometric quadriceps strength on a Biodex dynamometer. Patients were split at a TSK-11 score of 17, and second ACL injuries were tracked for 24 months with chi-square analysis.
paper.findings: High-fear patients (n = 19) had lower Marx activity in 73.7% versus 42.9% of low-fear patients (OR 3.73, 95% CI 0.98 to 14.23), single-leg hop for distance LSI of 95% or less in 55.6% versus 15% (OR 7.1, 95% CI 1.5 to 33.0), and quadriceps LSI of 90% or less in 50% versus 14.3% (OR 6.0, 95% CI 1.3 to 27.8); fear was not associated with the other hop tests. Fifteen patients (37.5%) had a second ACL injury; the ipsilateral group had higher TSK-11 scores than those without (19.8 vs 16.4, P = 0.03), and a score of 19 or more had RR 13.0 (95% CI 2.1 to 81.0) for ipsilateral tear. The TSK-11 had an AUC of 0.740 for ipsilateral injury, with sensitivity 0.75 and specificity 0.81, and was not associated with contralateral injury (P = 0.652).
paper.limitations: Only 40 patients from one institution, a pilot study with very few ipsilateral (8) and contralateral (7) injuries, so the RR and AUC are unstable. The activity association is not statistically clear (CI crosses 1), and the 90% and 95% LSI cut-offs are debated. The abstract Methods say patients were tracked for 12 months, but the Injury Tracking section and Results report 24 months. The population was young and active athletes planning to return to cutting and pivoting sports, and the authors did not control rehabilitation or surgeon return-to-sport criteria.
paper.practicalImplications: Asking athletes to complete the TSK-11 at clearance is quick and may flag those with higher fear who also show asymmetry or lower activity. The authors suggest fear may be worth considering in discharge planning, alongside hop and strength tests, but they do not give a validated cut-off for release.
paper.athleteDev: Higher fear scores at clearance went with lower self-reported activity at that time, though this association was not statistically clear. The data are not enough to change the training plan for an individual athlete.
paper.rtp: The paper directly informs return-to-sport decisions by suggesting that fear at clearance may be a discharge criterion for pivoting and cutting sports. The authors say this needs further study, and the study cannot establish a causal link or set a score that clears an athlete.

records.sourceFile: Sensorimotor Dysfunction Following Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury (Part 1) What Is It - How Can Clinicians Assess It.pdf

paper.citation: Vitharana TN, King E, Welch N, Devitt B, Moran K. Sensorimotor Dysfunction Following Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury (Part 1): What Is It? How Can Clinicians Assess It? Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2025.
paper.abstract: Clinical commentary asking what sensorimotor dysfunction follows ACL injury and how clinicians can assess it. Dysfunction is described across afferent pathways (pain and swelling, increased central processing, reduced proprioception, increased visual-motor reliance) and efferent pathways (reduced cortical and descending motor excitability, spinal reflex excitability acutely reduced then chronically increased). The authors propose practical tests of proprioception, pain, swelling, visual-motor reliance and processing, strength and voluntary activation.
paper.tldr: Sensorimotor dysfunction after ACL injury spans pain, swelling, proprioception, visual reliance and quadriceps activation, and most of it can be screened with simple clinic tests. The battery is expert-proposed and has not been validated against reinjury.
paper.methods: Narrative clinical commentary by five authors from sports medicine and university settings. The authors summarise mechanistic and clinical studies by subsystem (somatosensory, visual, efferent) and tabulate clinical tests with their equipment, facilitators and barriers. No literature search or appraisal method is described.
paper.findings: The authors cite knee proprioception deficits after ACLR compared with both the uninjured limb and healthy controls, including a joint position error of 7.2 degrees in the ACLR limb versus 1.9 degrees in the uninjured limb in 10 elite athletes. They cite increased visual cortex activity after ACLR and quadriceps voluntary activation deficits up to four years after surgery. For their own adapted stepdown test they report ICCs of 0.71 to 0.96 (unpublished) and that healthy athletes improved time to stability by 17% with eyes closed.
paper.limitations: No search or appraisal method, and the authors describe their recommendations as driven by clinical practice. The stepdown reliability and healthy-athlete data are unpublished, the suggested retest intervals (joint position sense every 4 to 6 weeks, strength every 6 to 8 weeks, EMG every 2 weeks) are practice-based, and the neurocognitive and sensory-station tests have no reliability data in ACLR patients. Most numbers quoted come from cited studies, not from new data.
paper.practicalImplications: Clinicians can track pain (VAS or NRS) and effusion (sweep or ballottement test) each session, joint position sense with an image-based method, quadriceps and hamstring strength by isokinetic or handheld dynamometry, and between-limb quadriceps activation with surface EMG. The authors cite isokinetic peak torque values for elite field-based athletes (quadriceps and hamstrings 3.19 and 1.78 Nm/kg in males, 2.32 and 1.36 Nm/kg in females) and a between-limb EMG difference above 22% to 30% as possibly clinically relevant.
paper.athleteDev: The cited strength values for elite field-based athletes can help frame late-stage strength targets after ACL injury. The article does not test whether reaching these values improves performance.
paper.rtp: The paper informs which sensorimotor domains to assess during ACL rehabilitation but proposes no return-to-sport criteria or cut-offs, and the visual-motor tests have no normative values or link to reinjury yet. It cannot be used as a clearance test battery.

records.sourceFile: Sensorimotor Dysfunction Following Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury (Part 2) - How Can Clinicians Rehabilitate It.pdf

paper.citation: Vitharana TN, King E, Welch N, Devitt B, Moran K. Sensorimotor Dysfunction Following Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury (Part 2): How Can Clinicians Rehabilitate It? Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2025.
paper.abstract: Clinical commentary reviewing methods to rehabilitate sensorimotor dysfunction after ACL injury and reconstruction. Rehabilitation should prioritise efferent function and somatosensory function while reducing reliance on the visual-motor system. Proprioceptive training should start within the first six weeks and be progressed by task, visual information, cognitive load and perturbation; cryotherapy and TENS are suggested early, and high-intensity strength training, NMES and EMG biofeedback throughout.
paper.tldr: Restore quadriceps drive with high-intensity strength work plus NMES and EMG biofeedback, and progress proprioceptive drills by task, vision, cognitive load and perturbation. These are expert recommendations from a narrative review, not tested protocols.
paper.methods: Narrative clinical commentary by the same author group as Part 1, combining cited intervention and mechanistic studies with the authors' sports medicine practice. It presents a framework for progressing proprioceptive drills and summary dosing guidance. No literature search or appraisal method is described.
paper.findings: The authors cite TENS reducing knee pain by 36% at specified settings, and cryotherapy with compression reducing pain by 50% with 83% of patients stopping pain medication by 6 weeks, versus 23% with standard ice packs. They cite increased corticospinal excitability when training at 75% but not 25% of maximum voluntary contraction, better quadriceps strength when NMES is added to exercise, and a progressive program building to over 90% of 1RM that brought ACLR athletes' strength to control levels by 7 months after surgery.
paper.limitations: No search or appraisal method, and recommendations combine cited evidence with clinical practice and mechanistic research. Several doses are extrapolated (stroboscopic dosing from skill-acquisition studies, excitability data from uninjured people), the three-sessions-per-week stroboscopic schedule is the authors' experience, and proprioceptive training after ACLR has not been tested. The summary calls the evidence for strength training, NMES and EMG biofeedback strong without any formal grading.
paper.practicalImplications: Early after surgery, the authors suggest cryotherapy with compression (ideally three times daily) for the first 6 weeks and daily 20-minute TENS for 4 to 6 weeks, with any medication prescribed by the treating physician. Throughout rehabilitation they recommend progressive strength training above 75% of 1RM, high-intensity NMES (15 to 20 s on, 15 to 50 s rest) and EMG biofeedback during strength sessions, plus proprioceptive drills progressed by task type, vision (including stroboscopic glasses), cognitive load and perturbation.
paper.athleteDev: The framework for adding visual, cognitive and perturbation challenges to landing, deceleration and change-of-direction drills can shape late-stage on-field rehabilitation. It has not been tested as a performance intervention.
paper.rtp: The paper guides rehabilitation content after ACL injury but gives no return-to-sport criteria or timelines and does not show that these methods reduce reinjury. It should not be used to decide clearance.

records.sourceFile: Should return to sport be delayed until 2 years after      ACL reconstruction - Biological and functional      considerations.pdf

paper.citation: Nagelli CV, Hewett TE. Should Return to Sport be Delayed Until 2 Years After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction? Biological and Functional Considerations. Sports Medicine. 2016.
paper.abstract: The authors argue that young, active athletes returning to high-level sport after ACL reconstruction have their highest second-injury risk in the first two years, and that the knee does not regain baseline biological and functional status until about two years. They postulate that delaying return to unrestricted sport to about two years would significantly reduce second ACL injuries.
paper.tldr: Young, active athletes after ACL reconstruction carry their highest second-injury risk in the first two years, while bone, graft, proprioception and strength are still recovering. The authors propose a return-to-sport delay of about two years for high-risk athletes.
paper.methods: This is a narrative review and opinion article (Sports Medicine) with no described search strategy or inclusion criteria. It draws on prospective and registry cohorts, imaging, proprioception, gait, hop-test and isokinetic strength studies after ACL reconstruction.
paper.findings: Second ACL injury risk is highest in the first two years after ACLR in young, active athletes, and the authors cite a second-injury rate of nearly one in three in the younger cohort. Bone bruises, graft ligamentization and proprioceptive and strength deficits are reported to approach baseline around two years, although the review notes conflicting evidence on proprioception and bone bruise relevance.
paper.limitations: The review has no described search method, so study selection cannot be reproduced. The two-year figure is an argued position, presented as a postulate, and the authors acknowledge that the relative contribution of sensory loss to second injury is unclear. Much of the cited evidence comes from observational cohorts and small samples.
paper.practicalImplications: Clinicians and staff can use the review to judge why early return may carry more risk for young athletes, and to weigh graft, bone and strength status in return-to-sport decisions. It does not establish a fixed two-year rule, because the delay is the authors' postulate and has not been tested as an intervention.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff should note that the review's argument for delayed return is about joint health and second-injury risk, not performance. The review does not provide training or performance outcomes for athletes returning from ACLR.
paper.rtp: The review directly addresses return to sport after ACLR, arguing for a delay of about two years for young, high-risk athletes. It should not be used to set a fixed date for an individual athlete, because it does not give validated readiness criteria or test the delay in a trial.

records.sourceFile: Similar Isokinetic Strength Preinjury and at Return to Sport after Hamstring Injury.pdf

paper.citation: van Dyk N, Wangensteen A, Vermeulen R, Whiteley R, Bahr R, Tol J, et al. Similar Isokinetic Strength Preinjury and at Return to Sport after Hamstring Injury. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2019.
paper.abstract: The study compared isokinetic strength of the injured hamstring at return to sport with pre-injury screening values in 41 professional male soccer players with MRI-positive hamstring injury. Injured-limb strength at return to sport averaged over 95% of pre-injury strength, and side-to-side differences were similar at return to sport and pre-injury. The authors conclude that isokinetic cut-off values are not useful for guiding strength restoration as a return-to-sport criterion.
paper.tldr: Hamstring-injured professional soccer players were about as strong at return to sport as before injury, and a greater than 10% strength difference was about as common before injury as at return. Isokinetic cut-offs should not be used alone to clear players to return.
paper.methods: Pooled data from two single-site randomized trials, including 41 players with MRI-positive hamstring injury who had pre-injury isokinetic screening. Concentric knee flexion and extension at 60 and 300 degrees per second and eccentric knee extension at 60 degrees per second were tested pre-injury, within seven days of injury (uninjured limb only) and before the return-to-sport assessment.
paper.findings: Injured-limb strength at return to sport averaged above 95% of pre-injury strength. The proportions with a >10% difference were similar at return to sport and pre-injury, and the only statistically significant changes (quadriceps and hamstring concentric strength at 60 degrees per second, differences of 4.9% and 5.3%) were small and within the minimal detectable change. Of the 41 injuries, 21 were grade I and 20 grade II, and one re-injury occurred in the completed trial.
paper.limitations: Testing was done at the end of a training session, so players may have been fatigued, and physicians were not blinded to the isokinetic results. Only grade I and II injuries were included, re-injury data are incomplete (one re-injury in the completed trial), and the population was homogeneous professional male soccer players. The authors suggest a 20% cut-point may be more realistic but say this needs further study.
paper.practicalImplications: Isokinetic strength should not be used alone as a return-to-play criterion or against a fixed 10% cut-off. Expect both deficits and surpluses in the injured leg at return, and interpret any difference against test variability, which the authors put above 20% for these measures.
paper.athleteDev: This study cannot guide training choices for performance. Its use is limited to reading isokinetic tests: differences of 10% are common in healthy and injured limbs alike, so small asymmetries should not be over-interpreted.
paper.rtp: Supports keeping isokinetic testing as one part of return-to-sport decisions, not a stand-alone criterion. It did not link strength at return to re-injury risk, because the re-injury data were incomplete.

records.sourceFile: Sport-related structural brain injury and return to play - Systematic review and expert insight.pdf

paper.citation: Zuckerman SL, Yengo-Kahn AM, Tang AR, Bailes JE, Beauchamp K, Berger MS, et al. Sport-Related Structural Brain Injury and Return to Play: Systematic Review and Expert Insight. Neurosurgery. 2021.
paper.abstract: Combines a focused PRISMA systematic review of sport-related structural brain injury from 2012 onward with a cross-sectional survey of 31 international sports neurosurgeons on operative management and return to play. The authors conclude that return-to-play decisions are heterogeneous and that level of play matters.
paper.tldr: Return to play after sport-related structural brain injury has no evidence-based guidance, and expert opinion varies widely. Experts allowed earlier return at higher levels of play, and most allowed high-contact sport at 6 to 12 months after resolved hemorrhage.
paper.methods: Focused systematic review following PRISMA, using PubMed MeSH terms and keywords; titles and abstracts from 2012 onward were screened, full texts reviewed by one author and verified by a senior author, and the protocol was not registered. A cross-sectional online survey covered 3 experience questions and 13 multiple-choice questions on operative indications and return timing in four scenarios at high school, collegiate and professional levels.
paper.findings: Of 241 records, 27 studies were included. Nine articles (12 athletes) reported return-to-play information, and 10 of those 12 cases were high school athletes or younger. Among 31 responding neurosurgeons, 12 (38.7%) would not operate on an acute, asymptomatic structural injury; midline shift over 10 mm (63.2%) and hemorrhage over 10 mm (52.6%) were the most common operative indications among those who would. For resolved hemorrhage, most experts allowed return to high-contact sport at 6 to 12 months, and about 80% did not endorse return to high-contact sport with persistent hemorrhage. After craniotomy, 40% to 50% considered return at 6 to 12 months. Linear regression found that experts allowed earlier return at higher levels of play (beta -0.58, P = .033).
paper.limitations: The systematic review yields little (27 studies, 12 athletes with return data), and the survey reflects opinion rather than outcomes. The regression is printed as beta -0.58 with 95% CI -0.111 to -0.005, which places the point estimate outside its own interval; this inconsistency appears in both the abstract and the results and should be checked against the source. The authors also note heterogeneity in both the literature and the survey responses.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the paper as a structured aid for individualized decisions rather than a return-to-play protocol. Note the authors' finding that experts were more lenient at higher competition levels, and that they were more conservative after craniotomy or with persistent hemorrhage.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: The review does not inform training load. Its only performance-relevant point is that expert views on return timing varied with level of play, so athletes at higher competition levels need individual planning with the treating neurosurgeon.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: Use it to frame the range of expert opinion on operative indications and return timing, such as 6 to 12 months for high-contact sport after resolved hemorrhage and no return for persistent hemorrhage in about 80% of experts. It cannot replace individual neurological and imaging assessment, and the evidence base is 12 athletes plus opinion.
